question_text: According to Sir Alexander Patterson (1957), quoted in the course material, "we are all in prison but in a matter of:
option_d: Choice, with no external constraint involved
explanation: Sir Alexander Patterson (1957) is quoted as saying "we are all in prison but in a matter of degree", meaning all people are constrained by norms and laws, though differing from those formally imprisoned for breaking them.

question_text: According to Berger (1973), quoted in the course material, society can be portrayed as a prison because "our bondage to society is not so much established by conquest as by collusion... we are entrapped by:
option_d: Purely economic factors with no social dimension at all
explanation: Berger (1973) portrays society as a prison, arguing our bondage to society is established by collusion rather than conquest: "we are entrapped by our own social nature", betrayed into captivity with our own cooperation.

question_text: According to Section 19 of the 1972 Act of Nigerian prisons, cited in the course material, a "prisoner" is defined as:
option_a: Any person lawfully committed to custody
option_b: Only a person convicted of a capital offence
option_c: Only a person who has confessed to their crime in writing
option_d: Only a person who has exhausted all rights of appeal
explanation: Section 19 of the 1972 Act of Nigerian prisons defines a prisoner as "any person lawfully committed to custody", also defining a sentence of imprisonment as any sentence involving confinement in a prison.

question_text: According to the course material, the spirit of Nigeria's present prison system is based on a very old prison ordinance of 1916, which enacted imprisonment with hard labor as the basis of treatment of offenders, with all Nigerian prisons currently administered under:
option_b: A treaty signed exclusively with the League of Nations in 1934
option_c: A single unified code enacted immediately upon independence in 1960
option_d: No formal legal instrument of any kind
explanation: The spirit of the present system is based on the old 1916 prison ordinance; at the time of the course's writing, all Nigerian prisons were administered under the Prison Decree No. 9 of 1972.

question_text: According to the course material, under the Nigerian traditional (pre-colonial) system, punishments were broadly of two types: fines, manual labor, compensation and restitution (applied without disturbing ordinary community life), and a second group comprising:
option_a: Death penalty and permanent banishment from the group
option_b: Only imprisonment in formal, purpose-built jails
option_c: Exclusively monetary fines, with no other form of punishment at all
option_d: A system entirely identical to the later British colonial system
explanation: Under the Nigerian traditional system, punishments were of two types: fines, manual labor, compensation/restitution, and corporal punishment applied without disturbing community life; the second, more serious group comprised death penalty and permanent banishment.

question_text: According to Ahire (1990), quoted in the course material, the attitude among many Nigerian jurists that the duty of criminal justice operators is merely to read, understand, and apply legal concepts rather than pose philosophical questions has fostered:
option_a: A wide gulf between legal knowledge and social realities
option_b: A perfectly harmonious and unified system of Nigerian jurisprudence
option_c: The complete elimination of all legal education in Nigeria
option_d: An immediate and total reform of Nigerian criminal law
explanation: Ahire (1990) argues that the attitude discouraging philosophical questioning among Nigerian jurists "has encaged the improvement and underdevelopment of legal education in Nigeria and fostered a wide gulf between legal knowledge and social realities".

question_text: According to Alf Ross (1929), cited in the course material, punishment can be defined in terms of four components, including that it occurs where there is a violation of a legal rule, is imposed by authorized persons on behalf of the legal order, involves suffering or unpleasant consequences, and:
option_b: Is always applied with no possibility of any error whatsoever
option_c: Occurs only in cases involving capital offences
option_d: Requires no formal judicial process of any kind
explanation: Alf Ross (1929) defines punishment through four components: violation of a legal rule, imposition by authorized persons on behalf of the legal order, involving suffering/unpleasant consequences, and expressing disapproval of the violation.

question_text: According to the course material, quoting Plato's Protagoras, "he who undertakes to punish with reason does not avenge himself for the past offence... he looks rather to the future and aims at preventing that particular person and others who see him punished from:
option_c: Receiving any form of legal representation
explanation: Plato, in the Protagoras, argued that reasonable punishment does not avenge a past offence but looks to the future, aiming to prevent the offender and others who witness the punishment from doing wrong again - the deterrence rationale.
